title: Encapsulation
description: Access modifiers, data hiding, and the getter/setter pattern for controlled field access.
objectives: Use private, public, and protected appropriately
Understand the purpose of data hiding
Write getters and setters that add validation

content.heading: Access Modifiers and Data Hiding
content.body:
Encapsulation means bundling an object's data together with the methods that operate on it, and restricting direct external access to that data — the core idea being that an object's internal state should only be changed in ways the object itself controls and validates. Java enforces this with access modifiers: private members are accessible only within their own class; public members are accessible from anywhere; protected members are accessible within the same package and by subclasses (even in other packages); and package-private (no modifier at all) is accessible only within the same package.

The conventional pattern is to make fields private and expose controlled access through public getter and setter methods — this lets a class validate any incoming value (a setter can reject a negative age, for instance) and lets the internal representation change later without breaking code outside the class that only ever used the getters/setters, not the raw fields.

content.heading: Getters, Setters, and Why It Matters
content.body: A getter typically follows the pattern getFieldName() (or isFieldName() for a boolean), simply returning the field's value. A setter, setFieldName(value), assigns the field, but critically can also validate: rejecting an invalid value, throwing an exception, or clamping it to a valid range, rather than blindly accepting whatever is passed in — something a public field could never do. This is why exposing public fields directly (bypassing encapsulation) is generally considered poor practice in Java: it removes any opportunity to enforce invariants about an object's own data.

content.explanation: balance can only be modified through deposit(), which validates the amount — a caller cannot set an invalid balance directly, since the field itself is private.

keyPoints: private restricts access to the declaring class; public allows access from anywhere
protected allows access within the package and by subclasses elsewhere
Fields are conventionally private, exposed through public getters/setters
Setters can validate input in ways a directly-exposed public field never could
commonMistakes: Making fields public 'for convenience', losing the ability to validate or later change the internal representation
Writing getters/setters that just pass values through with no actual validation, gaining little benefit over a public field
Confusing protected's actual scope (package + subclasses) with private's narrower one
